articles.title_zh: China is racing to the Moon, and America must clear the path for space innovation
articles.content_orig:
Silvia Inc. Chairman and CEO Anthony Pompliano discusses rumors of a potential merger between SpaceX and Tesla, Elon Musk's pledge to share stocks of his companies to American children and more on 'America's Newsroom.'
Since the dawn of civilization, mankind has looked to the stars and wondered: How did the universe come to be? What lies beyond our own world? Are we alone in this vast expanse? And will we ever venture far enough to set foot on another planet?
Over the centuries, human ingenuity has helped answer some of these questions. Others may only be known to our Creator. But whether mankind will ever live and work on another world is a question we are closer to answering now than ever before.
What once belonged to the pages of science fiction is rapidly becoming reality. And at the forefront of this extraordinary new era of exploration stands the United States of America.
PETER NAVARRO: TRUMP'S ARTEMIS VISION IS NOW FLYING — AND CHINA IS PAYING ATTENTION
From the Apollo program to today’s groundbreaking missions to the Moon and beyond, the American pioneering spirit has continually pushed the boundaries of what is possible. But what truly sets America apart is not simply the vision of our government or the brilliance of our scientists. It is the unmatched capabilities of our commercial space sector.
This image provided by Firefly Aerospace on Feb. 26, 2025, shows Firefly Aerospace’s Blue Ghost lunar lander orbiting the moon. (Firefly Aerospace via AP)
That success did not happen by accident. It is the product of decades of American innovation , investment and cooperation between the public and private sectors.
TRUMP TO TRANSFORM SPACEFLIGHT FROM SPECTACLE TO STATUS QUO TARGETING 3 LAUNCHES PER DAY
One of the clearest examples of what this partnership can accomplish is unfolding right in my home state of Texas.
In February 2024, Houston-based Intuitive Machines made history when its Odysseus lander became the first American spacecraft to touch down on the Moon in more than half a century — and the first privately built spacecraft to achieve a soft lunar landing. Just over a year later, Cedar Park, Texas-based Firefly Aerospace landed its Blue Ghost spacecraft on the lunar surface, delivering 10 NASA science and technology instruments and completing two weeks of operations.
NASA'S ARTEMIS FOLLOW-UP MISSION 'RIGHT AROUND THE CORNER' AFTER SUCCESSFUL LUNAR FLIGHT
These achievements are more than historic milestones. They demonstrate what is possible when NASA’s expertise and resources are paired with the talent and innovation of American companies. Through initiatives like NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services program, the federal government is helping develop a thriving commercial lunar industry while advancing the technologies needed to return astronauts to the Moon and eventually reach Mars.
As chairman of the House Science, Space, and Technology Committee , I have seen firsthand the role thoughtful policy can play in supporting these achievements. From commercial lunar deliveries to the next generation of space stations, our committee has worked to advance the partnerships, research and technologies shaping America’s future in space.
INNOVATION IS KEY TO AMERICA STAYING A SUPERPOWER. BUT IT IS MISSING AN ESSENTIAL PIECE
But the work is far from finished. As more nations recognize the economic and strategic importance of space, the United States faces growing competition, particularly from China . The future of exploration will be determined not only by what we accomplish in orbit or on the lunar surface, but also by where companies choose to invest, develop new technologies and build the infrastructure that makes those missions possible.
For America’s commercial space industry, the regulatory environment is a central part of that equation. Companies designing next-generation spacecraft, launch systems and other capabilities must navigate federal requirements that can affect everything from testing and licensing to operational deployment.
TRUMP SWINGS FOR MOON WITH NUCLEAR REACTOR PLANS AS CHINA, RUSSIA TEAM UP IN SPACE RACE
Our committee has a responsibility to build on this progress and ensure American space companies have the freedom to innovate and grow. That means examining outdated requirements, improving coordination across federal agencies and fostering an environment where the next generation of commercial capabilities can move from the drawing board to the launchpad.
We must also recognize what is at stake. As China sets its sights on expanding its presence beyond Earth, America cannot afford to become complacent. Our past achievements are no guarantee of future success. We should be making it easier for companies to build, invest and innovate here at home while working alongside allies and partners who share our commitment to peaceful exploration and a future in space guided by our shared principles.
These achievements are more than historic milestones. They demonstrate what is possible when NASA’s expertise and resources are paired with the talent and innovation of American companies.
The possibilities before us are nearly limitless. From establishing a lasting foothold on the Moon to sending the first humans to Mars, the next great chapter of our journey into space will depend on the ingenuity and resolve of the American people and the conditions we create for them to succeed.

articles.title_zh: Could Europe’s cost-of-living protests sharpen EU-China trade tensions?
articles.content_orig:
Unrest over economic hardship could strengthen calls to protect industry and jobs, though direct impact on trade talks is uncertain
As violent protests fuelled partly by the cost-of-living crisis shake parts of Europe, most notably France, analysts say the unrest could add to pressure on European policymakers to take a tougher trade stance towards China.
“One could argue that the EU looks weaker, but then one could also argue that there is more of a need to show external strength at a time of such events,” said David Henig, director of the UK Trade Policy Project at the European Centre for International Political Economy.
On Thursday, French President Emmanuel Macron said requests to hold protests submitted by people “with no legitimacy” would be banned in the coming days. Requests filed by unions would be examined under the law, while local authorities would propose alternative routes to keep demonstrations away from city centres, he said.

articles.title_zh: Duchess of Sussex ‘deeply distressed’ over child sexual abuse image claims against father
articles.content_orig:
Meghan also reveals she was made aware of ‘disturbing allegations’ against him in 2018 by Met police
The Duchess of Sussex has said she is “deeply distressed” over accusations involving child sexual abuse images against her estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr, and revealed she was made aware of “disturbing allegations” against him in 2018 by the Metropolitan police.
Meghan issued a statement after the Sun newspaper published claims that her half-brother Thomas Markle Jr alleged he had found a stash of images belonging to their father at his former home in the Philippines.
In an interview with the Daily Mail, Markle Sr denied possessing child sexual abuse images, calling the accusations “sick lies”.
It is understood that authorities in the UK had previously told Meghan that allegations made about her father in a 2018 letter sent to Scotland Yard, and subsequently shared with her by the police, were being investigated.
In a statement through her spokesperson, Meghan said: “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.
“In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.
“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them.
“I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.
“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.”
The 2018 letter was understood to have been shared with Meghan by the royalty and specialist protection unit within the Met police.
Markle Sr has been estranged from the duchess since he failed to attend her wedding to Prince Harry on health grounds, and has never met his grandchildren, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five.
The Sun reported that Markle Jr told detectives in the Philippines he had discovered “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images on computers and mobile phones stored in four large boxes at the home in Cebu where Markle Sr was living until he returned to the US in May after having a stroke.
Markle Jr, 60, said he had also contacted the FBI in the US, the Sun reported.
Meghan’s father has vehemently denied possessing child sexual abuse images, telling the Daily Mail that the accusations were “sick lies”.
He told the newspaper the computers had not been in his possession since he left Rosarito, Mexico, with his son in January 2025 and moved to the Philippines “for a fresh start”.
Speaking from a rehabilitation centre in Florida, where he is learning to walk with a prosthetic limb after his left leg was amputated because of a blood clot, he told the Mail: “I’m shocked, I’m hurt and I’m very upset that my son is making these accusations against me. I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.
“This is bullshit. It’s just a bunch of lies. It’s sick. I have no idea why Tom is trying to destroy me with these lies.”

London — Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, said in a statement sent to CBS News Friday that she was "deeply distressed" by reports that her father, Thomas Markle, is under investigation by authorities in the Philippines for alleged possession of child abuse materials.
Meghan, who recently moved back to Britain with her husband Prince Harry and their children, said she had been aware of allegations against her father since 2018, and that those allegations were shared with U.K. authorities at the time.
"In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated," her Friday statement said.
CBS News has sought comment from the London Metropolitan Police regarding Meghan's statement.
Meghan said she had distanced herself from her father in an effort to protect her children.
"I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them," she said.
The British tabloid The Sun reported Thursday that Thomas Markle, who has been estranged from his daughter for years , had been reported to authorities in the Philippines by his son, Thomas Markle Jr., after the younger man allegedly discovered child abuse materials in storage boxes at his father's home in the Philippines.
The Daily Mail reported Friday that Markle had denied the allegations against him.
"I have never downloaded anything like that in my life," he was quoted as telling the newspaper, as well as dismissing the allegations as "sick lies."
According to the Mail, Thomas Jr. made the discovery while his father was in the United States being treated for a stroke and blood clot. The son initially saw some of the materials after turning on an old cell phone at his father's home in the Philippines, and he subsequently reported the materials in July to an FBI hotline, as well as the National Center for Exploited and Missing Children and state police in Pennsylvania, according to the newspaper's report.
Philippines state media confrimed Friday, in a post shared on Facebook, that an investigation was underway.
"The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Friday said it is investigating reports involving an octogenarian American national who left child abuse videos and photos in his home in Cebu province," the state-run Philippine News Agency said.
A Filipino justice official said the department's anti-trafficking task force was investigating the matter and it confirmed that Thomas Markle Sr. was the subject of the investigation, according to the PNA report.
Meghan said in her statement that her "sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children."

articles.title_orig: Stock futures remain under pressure after worst Nasdaq session since June: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock futures remain under pressure after worst Nasdaq session since June: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
U.S. equity futures edged lower on Friday after tech stocks sold off on concerns that the artificial intelligence trade could be faltering, at least in the near term.
Futures tied to the S&P 500 were down 0.28%, Dow Jones Industrial Average futures were down 316 points, or 0.59%. Nasdaq-100 futures shed 0.1%
On Thursday, the Nasdaq Composite slid 2.6% and the S&P 500 sank 1.2%. The broad market benchmark posted its worst session since July, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq had its worst day since June. The Dow Industrials bucked the trend and closed marginally higher.
Worries around artificial intelligence spending weighed down the market and dragged the U.S. tech sector to a 3% decline on Thursday. Nvidia dropped 4.4%, Alphabet fell 3.2%, and Advanced Micro Devices declined 8.1% as losses occurred in different parts of the technology sector. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped 6.7% for its worst decline since June.
Chip stocks were rebounding slightly on Friday with Micron and Nvidia in the green. However, Big Tech shares like Microsoft and Meta were lower again in early trading.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC on Thursday he thought capital for the AI buildout was becoming constrained, which shined light on an ongoing concern about the rally: that the financing environment — not demand — could hold the AI trade back.
"There's a scarcity of capital. The demand [for] the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital," Huang said when asked about the neocloud segment of the AI buildout, which is proving to be fragile.
CoreWeave, which has become the poster boy for data center companies using aggressive amounts of borrowed money, dropped 10% on Thursday. The shares were flat in early trading Friday.
Ed Yardeni, president of Yardeni Research, described the AI trade on Thursday as a "bubble" but said that some depressurization wouldn't be all bad.
"Taking some air out of the AI bubble is a good thing. I don't think it's going to burst and create problems for the economy," he said, pointing to the bond market as a source of capital competition for equities.
The 10-year Treasury yield added 1 basis point to 4.9697% on Friday. The yield on the 30-year was flat and the 2-year yield fell 2 basis points. The upward moves come after Treasury yields fell sharply Thursday as investors looked to U.S. government bonds as a safe haven.
Oil prices also rose on Friday, further pressuring stocks. West Texas Intermediate futures were up 1.4% to $100.90 per barrel. Brent crude prices rose 0.75% to $114. It follows reports that the U.S. and Israel may be drawing up plans for renewed attacks on Iran as part of the regional war that started in late February.
On the week, the S&P 500 is heading for a slim gain, up less than 0.1%, while the Nasdaq is down 0.5% in the period. The Dow is tracking for a 1.7% advance.
On the economic front, traders will be watching for the final reading of the University of Michigan's consumer sentiment report.
Treasury yields edged higher early Friday, following a sharp drop in the previous session.
Yields on 10-year U.S. Treasurys — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — rose by 2 basis points to 4.9759%.
The yield on the 2-year Treasury note, which more closely follows short-term Federal Reserve rate decisions, also increased by 2 basis points to 4.6625%.  The yield on longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasurys — which tends to move on geopolitical developments — was up more than 1 basis point to 5.2985%.
Shares of Gucci-owner Kering fell 12% in early trading after the luxury company posted disappointing third-quarter earnings.
The move puts the stock firmly at the bottom of the pan-European blue-chip Stoxx 600 index, and brings 12-month losses to 43%.
Same-store sales declined by 1% overall, driven by a 6% decline for Gucci, its biggest brand and main moneymaker.
Kering, whose brands also include Saint Laurent, Bottega Veneta, and Balenciaga, has struggled more than peers amid a luxury slump.
Reigniting brand momentum at Gucci has proven particularly challenging against a difficult macroeconomic backdrop where consumers grapple with higher costs of living, Bernstein analyst Luca Solca said.
"A high dependency on newness to drive traffic and sales points to an underlying lack of interest in Gucci's core product," Solca added. "Unsurprisingly, management has stepped back from its initial outlook of a return to growth by the end of the year."
European luxury peers were also in the red on Friday morning, with conglomerate LVMH down 1.5%, Cartier-owner Richemont down 2.4% and Hermes falling 1.2%.
Hermes shares fell nearly 5% Thursday after reporting quarterly earnings, weighed down by soft demand in China.Kering
Asia-Pacific markets closed mixed on Friday.
South Korea's benchmark Kospi index added 0.3% to 5,550.3, while the tech-heavy Kosdaq index declined 1.62% to 751.69.
Japan's Nikkei 225 lost 0.34% to 62,693.16 and the broader Topix declined 0.79% to 3,965.81.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was flat at 8,795.2.
The CSI 300 rose 1.71% to end at 4,105.33, but closed lower for the week for an 11th straight time.
Third-quarter sales at L'Oreal topped forecasts amid stronger demand for premium hair and beauty products.
Total sales were 35.33 billion euros ($39.6 billion) for the three-month period, an adjusted like-for-like growth of 7.7% overall.
The French cosmetics group saw a particularly strong performance in Europe, where sales rose 9%, while revenue in South Asia and the Middle East rose 19.5% in the quarter. The company also saw a slight expansion in the beauty market in China.
"The global beauty market, once again, proved its resilience in a challenging context – and we continued to significantly outpace it," said CEO Nicolas Hieronimus, highlighting strong performances across all developed regions as well as e-commerce growth in emerging markets.
Shares were more than 3.7% higher in morning trade.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 was down 0.19% lower shortly after 8:10 a.m. in London (3:10 a.m. E.T.) with the continent's main sectors mixed, and regional bourses moving lower.
Oil and gas led morning gains, rising 1.24%, with household goods adding 0.56%, and bank stocks up 0.36%.
In Frankfurt, Germany's DAX led losses, falling 0.35%.In Paris, the French CAC 40 dropped 0.18% in early dealmaking, as the U.K. FTSE 100 slipped almost 0.1% in London.
Italy's FTSE MIB added 0.21% in Milan.
U.K. retail sales fell 0.4% in September from the previous month, a steeper drop than the 0.1% decline forecast in a Reuters poll. The fall partly reversed August's 0.7% rise and puts consumer spending in focus ahead of the government's budget on Oct. 28.
Despite September's decline, retail sales volumes rose 0.7% in the third quarter from the previous three months, the Office for National Statistics said Friday.
Phil Monkhouse, U.K. country manager at Ebury, said September's retail sales slide indicates a still-fragile consumer backdrop as households continue to grapple with rising prices and the prospect of higher borrowing costs.
"With the Autumn Budget less than a week away, uncertainty over potential tax changes adds another layer of caution for households and businesses alike," Monkhouse said in a note.
September's retail slide comes after U.K. GDP rose by 0.1% in August, which was driven mainly by services output.
Swedish defense giant Saab reported better-than-expected third-quarter earnings and revenue on Friday, as new orders more than tripled from a year earlier, boosted by a deal to supply Gripen fighter jets to Ukraine.
New orders came in at 65.8 billion Swedish kronor ($6.6 billion), up from 20.9 billion kronor a year earlier, beating FactSet expectations of 56.4 billion kronor.
The results come as European governments race to turn defense spending pledges into military capability.

articles.title_zh: 1 Thing in Bloom Energy’s Strong Earnings That May Be Dragging the Stock Down
articles.content_orig:

Bloom Energy reported record third-quarter revenue and a sharp increase in profitability on Thursday, driven by growing demand for its fuel cell technology as data centers and other energy-intensive industries seek reliable onsite electricity generation.
The California-based company posted revenue of $1.24 billion for the third quarter of 2026, a 138.1% increase from $519 million in the same period last year. Product revenue surged 179.4% to $1.07 billion, accounting for the bulk of the company's sales.
Net income attributable to common stockholders reached $250.3 million, reversing a $23.1 million loss a year earlier. Diluted earnings per share climbed to $0.78 from a loss of $0.10, while adjusted earnings per share increased to $0.94 from $0.15.
Profitability also improved significantly. Bloom's gross margin expanded to 33.8% from 29.2% a year earlier, while operating income jumped to $225.4 million from just $7.8 million.
The strong results prompted Bloom Energy to raise its full-year 2026 revenue forecast to between $4.4 billion and $4.6 billion, up from its previous guidance of $3.9 billion to $4.2 billion.
At the midpoint, the revised forecast represents approximately 122% annual revenue growth.
The company also increased its adjusted earnings guidance to $3.10–$3.40 per share and expects non-GAAP operating income of between $960 million and $1.03 billion.
The latest revision marks Bloom's third upward guidance adjustment this year, reflecting accelerating demand for its distributed power generation systems.
Bloom Energy's solid oxide fuel cells provide onsite electricity for data centers, semiconductor manufacturers, industrial facilities and other commercial customers.
The company has emerged as a major beneficiary of the artificial intelligence infrastructure boom, as hyperscale data center developers increasingly pursue alternatives to traditional grid-connected electricity supplies amid growing power requirements and grid connection constraints.
In June, Bloom and Brookfield Asset Management expanded their financing framework for AI-related power infrastructure from $5 billion to $25 billion, a fivefold increase from their original agreement announced in October 2025.
The expanded partnership is intended to support the deployment of Bloom's fuel cell systems for large-scale AI infrastructure projects, highlighting the growing investment flowing into distributed electricity generation.
Despite its earnings growth, Bloom reported negative operating cash flow of $27.1 million in the third quarter, compared with positive cash flow of $226.4 million in the preceding quarter. Capital expenditures also increased to $153.5 million from $51.6 million in the second quarter, underscoring the investment requirements associated with its rapid expansion.
Bloom also highlighted its addition to the S&P 500 index, marking another milestone for the fuel cell manufacturer as it scales its business to meet rising electricity demand.
The results reinforce the growing commercial importance of onsite power generation as AI development and industrial electrification place increasing pressure on conventional electricity infrastructure.

articles.title_orig: Hacking attempts rise after flaws found in program affecting 70 percent of websites
articles.title_zh: Hacking attempts rise after flaws found in program affecting 70 percent of websites
articles.content_orig:
The homepage of the PHP.net website is seen on October 22, 2026 in Singapore. Cyber-security flaws were recently identified in the popular PHP programming language, which is used on a vast number of websites across the world, including those of major companies and national governments. The PHP Foundation released two patches designed to fix the vulnerabilities. Yong Teck Lim/Getty Images hide caption
A few months ago AI caused global alarm after autonomous agents were found to have cheated on evaluations and then tried to cover it up, in what became known as the "Hugging Face hack."
This week, AI and hacking are back in the spotlight with AI technology credited to have helped prevent a global cybersecurity crisis.
Cyber-security firm Wiz Research, using OpenAI technology, announced on Wednesday it had discovered security flaws in a computer programming language that helps run some 70 percent of the world's websites.
OpenAI called the bug "one of the most impactful vulnerabilities in recent memory." Wiz Research warned that its "successful exploitation could allow attackers to take control of affected servers, steal sensitive data, and deface the websites running on them."
Corporations and governments from the U.K. to Japan are now rushing to prevent hackers from capitalizing on the flaws.
The flaws were discovered in a major programming language called PHP, short for Hypertext Preprocessor. Wiz Research calls PHP "the backbone of the web," saying the technology has underpinned much of the internet since the 1990s.
"These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history," the firm said, adding that before publicly disclosing the flaw, teams had worked on building a solution that's now available to websites to protect themselves.
As countries scrambled to prevent cyberattacks, numerous websites and pages were taken offline in the past few days. The U.S. National Security Agency warned organizations using PHP to "maintain heightened awareness" over the coming weeks. The U.K.'s National Cyber Security Center called on organizations to "take immediate action" to update their websites to the latest fixed or patched version.
Dozens of British and Finnish government services were taken offline this week. In France many local government sites were also briefly taken down. China's Industry Ministry urged entities to review security gaps.
In Japan, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi put out "an urgent request for everyone to take action," adding "If it is difficult to apply the fix patch promptly, temporarily suspending websites and similar measures can be considered an effective way to reduce risk."
Matthew Prince, the head of the cybersecurity firm CloudFlare, said his organization saw tens of thousands of attempts to exploit the flaw in the first 45 minutes of its discovery. That's now in the millions, Prince said on Thursday.
Wiz Research said the flaws in PHP had been present for decades.
"But demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve," the organization said. The AI models have "substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit. "

articles.title_zh: Japan university defence bids surge as post-war taboo fades amid China concerns
articles.content_orig:
Changing security norms and cash shortages push Japanese researchers to pursue state-funded defence tech projects
Japanese universities and other educational institutions more than doubled their applications for defence ministry research funding this year to a record 291, up from 123 last year, as Tokyo moves to strengthen its defence capabilities.
The increase is the clearest sign yet that academia’s decades-long resistance to military-linked work is diminishing.
The bids accounted for more than half the record 560 applications received by the ministry this year, up from 340 last year, with the rest coming from public research institutes and companies.
Of the 47 projects selected for funding under the 12.9 billion yen (US$82 million) programme, 30 will be led by university researchers, with 11 universities – including Osaka, Nagoya and Keio – winning grants for the first time.

articles.title_orig: AI is exposing security holes. The internet is freaking out and asking if it's time to pull the plug.
articles.title_zh: AI is exposing security holes. The internet is freaking out and asking if it's time to pull the plug.
articles.content_orig:
A few weeks ago, I heard a strange story about a friend who works at one of the Big Tech companies in Silicon Valley.
She'd recently ripped out the connected devices in her home, ordered paper bank statements, and stocked up on canned goods in her basement.
Now, she's a very sane, experienced person, and quite senior at one of the largest internet companies on earth. Why was she disconnecting so much? Just to be sure, my family ordered paper bank statements, too. It was still a head-scratcher, though.
Fast forward to this week, and her actions look a little less crazy.
AI models have exposed serious security weaknesses in software used by roughly 70% of websites. Meanwhile, US banks are finding AI agents inside customer accounts, including some that appear to be acting without their owners' instructions, Axios reported .
The digerati have now entered full freakout mode. Much of the internet meltdown is happening on, well, the internet, my colleague Alice Tecotzky noted.
On X and Reddit, warnings of a looming “Black October” spiraled into visions of AI grinding civilization to a halt. One lengthy post on X warned of a potential “global cyberattack/AI swarm” and offered a survival checklist: Stockpile cash in small bills, print out your neighbors' phone numbers, download maps, buy a hand-crank radio, and stash a gallon of water per person per day.
Oh, and don't forget the manual can opener. You don't want to survive the AI apocalypse only to be defeated by a tin of beans.
Nikita Bier , a prominent app developer and former head of product at X, best captured the mood.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
"It's time to turn off the internet," he posted Wednesday night .
If you're reading this, you haven't done that yet. But should we really be worried?
I put that question to Stephanie Cohen , chief strategy officer at Cloudflare, which helps protect about 20% of the internet.
"The world is a little bit scary right now," she told me on the side of Cloudflare's annual conference in San Francisco this week.
Here's the problem. The internet is built on decades of software, much of it riddled with security holes.
Some of these weaknesses have been known for years. However, fixing them takes time and money, and hackers often lacked the skills to exploit them anyway. So they were left alone.
AI changes that calculation dramatically. Someone who previously needed years of training to break into a computer system can now get help from an AI model. And these tools can search for weaknesses at a speed humans simply can't match.
The result: The number of newly published software vulnerabilities ( Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures in industry lingo) has exploded.
Now, there's a frantic race between people trying to break into systems and those trying to protect them.
Cohen's message, though, was surprisingly reassuring.
AI helps the good guys find and fix these problems. Cloudflare, for instance, released protections for the latest vulnerability to customers, including those using its free service.
And there's a bigger effort underway.
OpenAI has launched an initiative called Patch the Planet, working with Cloudflare and other security professionals to use AI to find weaknesses in widely used software and help repair them.
Tom Occhino , chief product officer at Vercel, told me recently that his company has been talking with partners about launching a nonprofit that would fund a swarm of good AI agents that go out on the internet to find and fix software flaws.
Amazon is joining the fight, too. Its new Continuum service, available Thursday, uses AI agents to find security holes and propose fixes. Amazon said that people maintaining freely available software can use it to help protect the wider internet.
Humans may still have to check and approve these repairs, but the prospect of AI helping clean up decades of neglected software is encouraging.
The irony of this is not lost on some in the industry.
"The funny thing is everyone was saying AI slop code will cause a cyber crisis but it's actually all the old human slop causing it and the AI is just cleaning it up," software engineer Ben Kaufman wrote on X on Thursday.
Either way, Cloudflare's Cohen thinks these AI-inspired freakouts will push the industry to do better — by exposing issues and adding urgency to get them patched.
"We may end up in a world where actually we've become significantly more secure at the end," she said.
The trouble is getting there.
When I ran into Occhino recently at a Vercel conference in San Francisco, he described a world in which software that everyone assumed was safe suddenly looks vulnerable because increasingly capable AI models are scrutinizing the basic systems that underpin the internet.
That led to a more fundamental discussion between us: Why did we connect so many things to the internet in the first place?
For years, the technology industry has raced to put everything online. Thermostats. Refrigerators. Doorbells. Cars. Bank accounts.
We assumed that connecting something to the internet automatically made it better.
Perhaps we should reconsider.
I remember the world before the internet. It worked pretty well. We managed to buy groceries, pay bills, heat our homes, and generally get through the day without every appliance talking to a computer somewhere.
That doesn't mean abandoning online banking or throwing your smartphone into the sea.
Occhino, for one, isn't particularly worried about hackers wiping out his bank account. Modern banks have sophisticated protections, and he recommends everyone turn on additional login security.
Maybe the cybersecurity crowd, which spends its life immersed in online threats, is missing something obvious.
Not everything needs to be connected.
Occhino put it neatly: "There's certain things that don't make sense to be on the internet in the first place."
Perhaps that's the lesson from this week's panic. We don't need to turn off the internet.
We just need to remember where the off switch is.

Beijing called on Washington on Friday to respect market economy rules and stop disrupting the normal economic and trade cooperation between companies, following the United States Treasury Department's proposed restrictions on US investment in Chinese biotechnology sector.
The proposal, which, if finalized, would be the first restrictions on foreign investment in the pharmaceutical industry, prohibits transactions covering "certain bio-derived compounds or materials", biomanufacturing equipment and facilities, and technology related to biological design and sequencing, the Politico reported.
Overstretching the concept of national security, adopting discriminatory measures against specific countries, and restricting trade and investment activities serve neither side's interests, Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said on Friday.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine says two soldiers died after arrested girl sent Russian poison
articles.title_zh: Ukraine says two soldiers died after arrested girl sent Russian poison
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian police said Friday they had detained a 17-year-old girl suspected of helping Russia's security services to poison Ukrainian soldiers and that two had died.
Ukraine and Russia have throughout their war since 2022 accused each other of recruiting minors for sabotage acts including poisoning.
The girl, who was not named, is suspected of having packaged deadly drugs and sending them to Ukrainian soldiers she contacted by Telegram, said a police statement.
She was arrested by police in Zhytomyr, west of Kyiv, after allegedly following instructions from a Russian handler in exchange for at least 5,000 hryvnias ($111), they said.
After receiving packages with "free drugs", the soldiers were "instructed to take them on camera", the statement said.
"The recipients did not know that the capsules contained a lethal dose of methadone," it said, adding that "two soldiers died from poisoning in the Zhytomyr region."
Police said they had identified other recipients of the packages, which "prevented four more murders" across the country.
"The young woman was notified that she is suspected of aiding and abetting the premeditated murder of two people as part of a prior conspiracy," the police statement said.
She was also suspected of "shipping drugs and psychotropic substances for the purpose of distribution", it said, adding that she faced up to 15 years in jail if found guilty.
Police cautioned that Russia aims "to kill our people and destabilise the situation within the country".
"Do not accept medication or other substances, as well as food or drinks of dubious origin, from people you do not know well," police cautioned.
Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, Ukrainian authorities say they have opened thousands of investigations into collaboration with the enemy, and frequently arrest individuals accused of working for Moscow.
In 2023, Ukraine accused Russia of poisoning the wife of Kyrylo Budanov, who was then head of Ukraine's military intelligence and is now a presidential advisor.

articles.title_orig: Final Israeli polls point to stalemate ahead of Tuesday’s election
articles.title_zh: Final Israeli polls point to stalemate ahead of Tuesday’s election
articles.content_orig:
With no more polls allowed to be released before the election, neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition is reaching the 61-seats necessary for an outright majority
ack GUEZ / AFP via Getty Images
A road sign stands in front of a large billboard featuring Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu (R) of the Likud party and former military chief and leader of the centrist Yashar party, Gadi Eisenkot, in Ramat Gan on October 20, 2026.
The likeliest outcome of Israel’s upcoming election is a stalemate , according to the final polls ahead of next Tuesday’s election, with neither side — Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc and the bloc opposing him, led by Gadi Eisenkot — projected to reach a majority of the Knesset.
Israeli law prohibits the publication of new polls from Friday until the Oct. 27 election.
The overall polling average put the bloc led by Netanyahu ahead, with 54 seats, while the opposition would get 50 seats, both short of the necessary 61-seat majority. Netanyahu’s Likud polled at 23 seats compared to 21 for Eisenkot’s Yashar party.
However, the gap between polls from right-leaning news outlets and those from the mainstream networks and publications was significant.
In the average of six mainstream TV and newspaper polls, the Eisenkot-led bloc had more seats than the current coalition. An average of polls from the last two days showed Eisenkot’s bloc narrowly ahead, holding 52 seats to the Netanyahu bloc’s 50 seats.
Meanwhile, an average of the polls on Israel’s Channel 14 and i24 News — which rely, respectively, on Shlomo Filber, a former Netanyahu campaign aide, and Direct Polls, the firm Filber founded with former Likud strategist Tzuriel Sharon before departing last year — found Netanyahu’s coalition projected to receive a 61-seat majority of the Knesset, while Eisenkot’s bloc would only have 45 seats. Those polls have been outliers, but Direct Polls was the most accurate in the last election.
The Arab parties, the Joint List and Ra’am, are polling at an average of 14 seats, just short of their record 15 seats in 2020 when they ran together. Leading figures in both blocs have vowed not to include Arab parties in their coalition.
Arab voter turnout has hovered around the 50% mark in the last decade. However, Stat-Net, a polling institute specializing in the Israeli Arab population, has said that it may be as high as 68-69% this year, which may give the parties representing the Arab minority even more seats than projected.
Increased Arab turnout would contribute to higher overall turnout, which would increase the number of votes needed to meet the minimal threshold to enter the Knesset.
In both the general polling average and the right-leaning media’s polls, neither Amcha Yisrael nor the Reservists and Economy Party, which have hovered near the 3.25% electoral threshold in recent weeks, received enough votes to enter the Knesset. In the more left-leaning polls, Reservists and Economy, which has not pledged to recommend either Netanyahu or Eisenkot for prime minister, receives an average of three seats.
An Israel Democracy Institute poll found that Israelis would rather have another election than alternative ways of handling a stalemate. Over a third of Jewish Israelis (35%) and nearly half (46%) of Arabs preferred a repeat election, whereas 28% of Jews and 9% chose a unity government with a rotation for prime minister, and 23% of Jews and 25% chose a minority government.

articles.title_orig: Hundreds of flights cancelled across East Asia as Typhoon Champi roars toward Taiwan
articles.title_zh: Hundreds of flights cancelled across East Asia as Typhoon Champi roars toward Taiwan
articles.content_orig:
Taiwan is bracing for Champi's worst effects on Saturday
Hundreds of flights in the East Asia region were cancelled on Friday as powerful Typhoon Champi roared close to Taiwan's north-east coast.
Schools and offices in Taiwan were shut as Champi neared the island. While it is uncertain if it will make landfall, the storm was forecast to bring 90cm (35in) of rain and strong winds to the north-east until Saturday.
One person died after being swept away by waves, authorities said. The storm also injured 171 people and forced 1,000 others to evacuate.
Champi is the latest in a string of intense typhoons as a Super El NiÃ±o heats up the Pacific Ocean and fuels storms. At its peak earlier this week, it was the planet's strongest storm of the year so far.
On Friday afternoon, Champi was packing wind gusts of 191km/h (119mph) .
After passing Taiwan's north-eastern tip and the Okinawa islands in southern Japan, Champi is expected to hover over the waters off China's eastern coast, before curving farther to the north-east to Japan's main island.
Weather agencies in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Japan forecast that the eye of the storm is expected to pass without making landfall in Taiwan,
However, a forecaster in Taiwan's Central Weather Administration told Reuters that they could not rule this out completely - especially if the storm "stalls, loops or wobbles from side to side" as it approaches.
Rainfall is expected to peak on Saturday morning and continue to batter Taiwan until Saturday evening, the Central Weather Administration said.
Taiwanese authorities have urged people to stay away from coasts and mountains.
Work and classes were suspended in nearly all of Taiwan's 22 counties and cities on Friday - what's colloquially known as a "typhoon holiday" - as Champi approached the island.
Taiwan's $5tn (Â£3.7tn) stock exchange was also closed on Friday because of the severe weather.
Only Kinmen county, an archipelago located to the west of Taiwan's main island, continued work and classes as usual.
In Japan, power cuts were reported in nearly 8,400 households in the southern Okinawa prefecture, according to the local power company.
More than 160 flights have been cancelled across four Japanese airlines.
Champi has also stirred up heavy rains and winds in Batanes, a Philippine island chain below southern Taiwan.
Photos posted on the local government's Facebook page showed waves crashing into seaside villages and roads closed to traffic. There were no immediate reports of casualties.
Typhoon Champi became the strongest storm of the year earlier this week, when it attained a maximum sustained wind speed of 185mph (298km/h) as it moved over the Philippine Sea - the equivalent of a Category 5 hurricane.
While initially categorised as a "super typhoon", Champi weakened on Wednesday as it continued barrelling through the sea.
This is shaping up to be one of the most active typhoon seasons the region has seen in years. Champi is Japan's 30th typhoon of the year - making this the first time since 2013 that the country has seen so many storms.
The recent frequency of storms is due to an unusually strong El NiÃ±o - a naturally occurring phenomenon that hits the Pacific Ocean every few years and can trigger extreme weather events, from droughts to typhoons.

Two Palestinian gunmen killed and five Israelis wounded near Hebron days ahead of a tight Israeli election
Suspected Palestinian militants wounded five Israelis on Friday before two gunmen were killed in a prolonged shoot-out, leading Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to order the closure of the West Bank days before Israeli elections.
Netanyahu, facing a tight race for a new term in Tuesday’s election, said that Israeli troops prevented what could have been a major attack, with the assailants allegedly carrying a large quantity of ammunition in their vehicle.
An Agence France-Presse journalist who witnessed the firefight saw two Palestinian men in casual attire and armed with a handgun and an automatic rifle exchanging fire with Israeli forces at a checkpoint near the Palestinian city of Hebron.

At least 16 people were killed and 32 more injured when a strong 7.0-magnitude earthquake struck China’s western Tibet autonomous region late on Thursday, state news agency Xinhua said, citing local authorities.
More than 300 houses collapsed in the earthquake, which struck on Thursday at 10.33pm. Officials were still evaluating the damage, and disaster relief work was ongoing, Xinhua said.
The epicentre of the quake was located in a mountainous area about 190km (120 miles) east-northeast of Nagqu and 390km northeast of the regional capital Lhasa, the US Geological Survey said.

articles.title_orig: From Buenos Aires to Colombo, discontent simmers under the surface of rebounding economies
articles.title_zh: From Buenos Aires to Colombo, discontent simmers under the surface of rebounding economies
articles.content_orig:
Published by Global Banking & Finance Review
Posted on October 23, 2026
Â· Last updated: October 23, 2026
By Libby George, NicolÃ¡s Misculin and Uditha Jayasinghe
LONDON/BUENOS AIRES/COLOMBO, Oct 23  (Reuters) - Gustavo Raul Perez furrows his brow over a notebook at the hardware shop he has run for six years on the outskirts of Buenos Aires.
Since Javier Milei became president of Argentina in 2023 â with Perez's vote â rapid reforms have thrilled investors and won praise from the International Monetary Fund. Perez, though, mainly feels the pinch.
"This economic plan is for a few," he said.
Inflation has fallen to roughly 33% from nearly 300%, imports have opened up and subsidies have fallen.
But Perez's restocking costs have tripled and customers have less to spend.
"There was a middle class three years ago," he says. "It doesn't exist anymore."
Perez's experience reflects a tension coursing through emerging economies: reforms that restored investor confidence and stabilised public finances have yet to improve living standards for many.
In Morocco, glittering new office towers contrast with frustration on city outskirts. In Sri Lanka, economic crisis and debt default have subsided but poverty remains above pre-crisis levels.
From fuel subsidy removal in Nigeria to privatisation in Egypt and market opening in Uzbekistan, years of reforms have helped emerging economies weather shocks â yet often grate with citizens who hear of economic turnarounds that do nothing for them.
Nigeria's finance minister warned failing to address inequality is like "sitting on gunpowder". Morocco's central bank says stubborn unemployment has widened the gap between economic performance and citizens' perceptions.
"When people in emerging markets are faced with rising food, fuel and energy costs...that is what they feel immediately," says Torbjorn Soltvedt of Verisk Maplecroft, warning that unrest and instability could follow. Indeed, average global civil unrest risk hit its highest in nearly a decade this year, according to his company.
The IMF and investors have long pressed emerging economies to reduce subsidies and currency controls.
The pandemic, then food and fuel spikes after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, jolted many into action: cutting spending, liberalising exchange rates and hiking interest rates.
Removing subsidies and weakening currencies raises prices even as spending cuts squeeze incomes â but leaders had "absolutely no other choice," says Simon Quijano-Evans of Macro Hive, or they risk an "abyss" of lost investment.
The changes drew investors back; emerging economies now grow around 4%, roughly twice the pace of advanced economies.
But if public anger derails reform, these countries risk losing more than confidence â backsliding could stall the investment and job creation needed to narrow the gap with richer nations.
In Morocco, foreign direct investment flow nearly doubled last year, but deadly youth-led protests rocked the country, and in July hundreds of would-be migrants flocked into a neighbouring Spanish enclave.
"Morocco is developing at two different speeds," civil engineer Anass Sayad said while walking with his family in Casablanca Finance City. He pointed to stadiums and skyscrapers while saying that education and healthcare deserve more attention. The government boosted spending on both in its 2026 budget, though any impact will take time to reach its citizens.
The World Bank estimates 1.2 billion people in developing countries will reach working age over the next decade â raising doubts over whether investment will create enough jobs for them.
IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva warned higher fuel and food costs and declining development assistance were piling on pressure despite years of "hard work", while the Fund called for more low-income country support.
Anger and unrest are not confined to emerging economies; cost-of-living pressures have brought protesters onto the streets of France, Italy and Spain.
But wealthy countries have greater fiscal firepower to cushion households. In developing economies inflation can also bite harder, with food accounting for 30% to 50% of consumer price baskets, compared with 13% to 14% in the US.
In Colombo, food vendor Sirimodara Wadaramge Sriyakanthi wakes before 5 a.m. to prepare herbal porridge and rice packets for lunch, absorbing higher costs to keep her prices near $2.
"I sell the lunch packets at a reasonable price so people can afford it," she says, worrying about her son's school fees and daughter's dance lessons.
Sri Lanka may have emerged from crisis â but to her, little feels different.
"We have so many expenses," she says.
($1 = 331.3500 Sri Lankan rupees)
(Additional reporting by Abdelhak Balhaki in Casablanca and Miguel Lo Bianco in Buenos Aires, editing by Karin Strohecker and Hugh Lawson)

articles.title_zh: The revolution arrives in Albania This is Europe’s autumn of discontent
articles.content_orig:
Gone is the summer’s disaffection with Edi Rama, replaced by a burning, visceral hatred. (Aris Roussinos)
Gone is the summer’s disaffection with Edi Rama, replaced by a burning, visceral hatred. (Aris Roussinos)
Outside the locked gates of Tirana’s Catholic Cathedral last Saturday, a riot policeman ran towards me with his club upraised to bash me on the head. When I shouted that I was English — it was not the moment for the interminable navel-gazing of current British political discourse — he wavered for a second, then shoved me out of the way instead. Camera in hand, I had interrupted him and his colleagues as they attempted to beat, through the railings, a handful of teenage protesters who had run through thick clouds of choking tear gas into Church grounds for sanctuary. A few moments earlier, black-clad rioters outside the cathedral had hurled petrol bombs at the policemen, as they tried to charge across the pedestrian Vodafone Bridge. After the police withdrew, to chase other protesters, I spoke to a crying teenage girl, being comforted by a gray-haired nun beneath the bronze statue of Mother Teresa. “They have such hatred in their eyes, we are just protesting for our rights, we have done nothing wrong,” the girl said, shaking. “This is all because the government is not listening to us, is not doing anything to help us, to help any of the poor people of Albania, in any way,” said the nun, visibly furious, her eyes red-rimmed from tear gas. It was the fifth, and most violent day so far, of the student-led protests that have plunged Albania’s capital into chaos for over a week.
Since May, Tirana’s central boulevard had been the scene of the peaceful, and joyful “Flamingo Revolution” protests , named after the animals supposedly threatened by the Kushner-led coastal development project in the southern village of Zvërnec. But if the “Flamingo Boulevard” of the summer was a protest movement that styled itself as a revolution, what is happening now is an attempted revolution that styles itself as a student movement. The demonstrators are attempting to overthrow Edi Rama’s Socialist Party government, elected for a fourth consecutive term only last year, with the aim of installing a caretaker technocratic government before new elections. On Saturday, it looked for a dramatic few hours like they might succeed. Thousands of protesters had filled Tirana’s main boulevard, pressing right up to the Prime Minister’s Office, Albania’s seat of government. Masked and black-clad youths kept pushing forward with howls of joy and rage against the water cannon and shield walls of riot police, cheers going up as petrol bombs exploded in flames against the armored trucks, forcing them to retreat. If the underlying causes — an end to political corruption, greater social spending, an entirely new political system — are the same as before, the mood among the protesters has become newly fierce. Gone is the summer’s disaffection with Edi Rama, replaced by a burning, visceral hatred.
Whenever the rioters wavered, chants of “Down with the dictator, Down with the communists” rang out, motivating them to push forward once again into the thick clouds of tear gas, hurling back the CS canisters, and aiming fireworks at the police ranks. Hijacking a parked car, the protesters rolled it towards the police lines and set it aflame, forcing the police to retreat. Young women in gym wear and Covid masks, and young men in black tracksuits and ski masks ran as close to the police as they could to hurl their missiles, jeering and cursing at them, the men often thrusting their groins at their opponents to indicate, in a manner it does not take a fluent command of Albanian to understand, what they wished to do to the officers. Dozens of times that Saturday night, I had to escape from the choking tear gas; every time, within seconds, a volunteer ran up to squirt distilled water in my eyes, an indication of the impressive and seemingly organic level of student organization behind the protests. Tea, a 21 year old math student, asked me where I was from as she squirted water into my eyes. England, I spluttered. “Then you don’t know us Albanians, we are crazy as fuck,” she laughed. “He is going, and we are going to make him go, as quickly we can.”
At a pavement cafe near the protests, I met Genc Pollo, a prominent conservative intellectual and politician, and a strong critic of Rama’s government. An urbane figure, it was a surprise to see him with swimming goggles perched on top of his head, an attempt to keep out the tear gas from the protests he now observes nightly. If the Flamingo protests had been listened to by the government, he told me, all this violence could have been avoided. “But the answer from the government was mostly derision, mockery, calling them foreign spies, calling them algorithmic manipulators, and the usual stuff.” Instead of concessions, “immediately, with the police, replying with tear gas and batons, and now rubber bullets, it turned into a violent confrontation. That is “a very logical evolution of the situation. Should the frustration, and the discontent, and the legitimate grievances have been really dealt with, not with decoys, not with propaganda, and on the top of that, derision for the protesters, it could have been channeled into peaceful ways, peaceful solutions, and arrangements.” Was there a solution that ends with Rama still in power? “I don’t think that’s possible,” Pollo told me. “Since it has become tense and also violent, I don’t think it will last as long as the Flamingos. By the nature of it, I mean if it’s either way, it will be decided in a shorter time frame.”
Back on the boulevard, beneath the din of the tear-gas grenades, I asked Jurgen, a  20-year-old law student, why he was here. “Because of the corrupt government and everything that has been happening in the past 13 years,” he told me “The PM will resign, hopefully this weekend, because of the mass protests, he should reflect on that. We gave him 140 days of just asking nicely, he didn’t listen, so now things took a turn. This is the result of not listening to the people of Albania. I cannot name a single thing he’s done that has benefited me as a student or as an Albanian.” Behind him, a group of older women, one in a hijab, were busy tearing up the cobbled pavement and filling a wheeled shopping trolley with rocks to be trundled towards the young men at the front. Indeed, for a Gen-Z protest, there were a surprising number of men with gray hair at the forefront of the clashes, hurling rocks and metal poles at the police lines.
While the violence is led by students and schoolchildren, the polite middle-class protestors of the summer have been joined by older toughs, with indications that ultras from Tirana’s football firms have set aside their rivalries to unseat their embattled Prime Minister. To the chants of “Rama resign” and “Rama to jail, Berisha to jail” from the peaceful summer protests have been added a new one: the slogan of the Balli Kombëtar , the Right-wing Second World War resistance movement: “Albania for Albanians, Death to Traitors.”
For many protesters, however, it is contemporary geopolitics that most concerns them. “Rama will go,” one man in his 30s told me, “but he will only go when other nations, America and Europe force him to go, because he has a bad personality, he is difficult, and also because he is implicated with criminal gangs, and with Israel.” If the Kushner-led Zvërnec project was the spark for the summer Flamingo protests, a broader sense that the Rama government is too close to Israel has led to widespread conspiracy theories that Tel Aviv has sent reinforcements and crowd control equipment to the Albanian police, and that Rama has sold the country out to Israeli interests. Among the many demands for revolution scrawled along the walls of the boulevard was the terse spray-painted message: “Fuck the Jew Rama.” In a country that is fiercely nationalistic even

CCTV says the proposed measures are intended to establish clearer regulatory boundaries rather than shut the door on Chinese AI tech exports
Chinese artificial intelligence model developers DeepSeek and MiniMax have completed export registration procedures and proceeded with open-source releases and overseas licensing activities, according to Chinese state media, days after Beijing moved to tighten oversight on AI tech transfers.
The draft proposal released by the Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) and Ministry of Science and Technology, which also included provisions that came into immediate effect requiring official registration for the covered technologies, raised questions about whether Beijing was restricting Chinese AI companies from expanding overseas, particularly as the country’s open-weight models have gained international adoption.

articles.title_orig: What smart people are saying about AI unleashing an online 'vulnerability tsunami'
articles.title_zh: What smart people are saying about AI unleashing an online 'vulnerability tsunami'
articles.content_orig:
It's been a nightmarish week for cybersecurity.
AI helped discover two "critical" flaws in the infrastructure of PHP , a programming language that up to 70% of websites use, prompting companies to race to roll out a fix or risk being hacked.
The incident has illustrated how AI is creating a new level of risk for businesses and consumers online, in a week when multiple other cyber threats caused headaches for security workers.
Here's what executives and analysts are saying about the biggest cyber threat of the moment — and how AI could make things even worse.
Anthropic's deputy security chief, Jason Clinton, warns that a "vulnerability tsunami" is coming — and says critical infrastructure hasn't caught up.
Clinton posted on X on Wednesday about the need to "patch critical infrastructure" before core network vulnerabilities get exploited. On Thursday, he issued another warning to companies.
"As bad as things have gotten in the past 4 days, they are going to get a lot worse before they get better," he wrote.
"Security leaders, never let a crisis go to waste: please go to your boards and ask for help right now. not for ai, for the basics. (we need to hold on for ~18 months.)," he added.
Andrew Curran, a prominent AI analyst, weighed in on several cybersecurity threats from Wednesday to Thursday.
"Regarding potential attacks on energy, food, and water infrastructure, the threat is quite real. Someone is currently probing infra and feeling it out, it is an active threat. Even a little preparation can be helpful, just in case," Curran wrote on Wednesday in response to an NSA cybersecurity advisory about threat actors.
On Thursday, Curran also highlighted a hack of Quest Diagnostics, which he said serves "roughly half" of the US's hospitals and physicians.
In February, Matt Shumer, the former CEO of Hyperwrite, published a viral essay on his website titled "Something Big Is Happening," in which he warned of large-scale disruptions wrought by AI that could upend the world order.
Shumer published another essay on Thursday on his website and LinkedIn, this time titled "The Internet Is Under Attack. Here's How to Protect Yourself and Your Family."
"Right now, as you read this, swarms of AI agents are likely trying to break into the websites you use. Not one of them. Many of them," Shumer wrote. "We are in the middle of the biggest cybersecurity moment in years."
This is what could happen, per Shumer's post:
Shumer also outlined four ways people can protect themselves, including updating all their software and staying off sites they're unfamiliar with while companies and websites alike make their security updates.
He also advises that people protect their bank accounts by being extra cautious about any and all codes and links that they receive. People should also "close the doors you aren't using" by unplugging smart gadgets and deleting apps that aren't being utilized.
"Every connected thing is another way in," Shumer wrote.
Marc Benioff agreed with Anthropic's Jason Clinton in an X post on Thursday.
"Jason is 100% right. Code red," Benioff wrote, along with a red alarm emoji.
Sriram Krishnan, a prominent venture capitalist and former senior AI policy advisor for President Donald Trump, said that the PHP vulnerabilities are a "harbinger of things to come" as AI models continue to detect long-standing cyber issues.
"However the entire software supply chain will need the muscles to rapidly build and deploy fixes," he said in a post on X.
The new cyber reality may require more public-private partnerships to build the required infrastructure, he said.
The Menlo Venture partner Deedy Das warned that "the era of vibe hacking is here" in a series of posts on X.
He said he'd seen firsthand that "even non-technical people" can exploit common vulnerabilities, such as PHP, using AI models. Das said someone could theoretically direct certain models to any website and instruct them to quickly locate the vulnerabilities.
"Once you figure it out, it is downright trivial to do. The digital infrastructure of the world is at risk," he wrote.
AI agents have ended the era of "security through obscurity" because they can devote once-unthinkable time and effort to finding vulnerabilities, Box CEO Aaron Levie said on X. People will need to upgrade legacy infrastructure, modernize security policies, and tighten access controls, among other measures, he said.
"Agents will help on the defensive side because they can both accelerate this work and equally simulate the risk vectors," Levie wrote.
Yet Levie thinks humans also have an important role to play in the cyber revolution — he predicted a boom in cybersecurity jobs , which could become a huge investment area for companies.
"You will need more talent to point the agents at the most critical work, review findings, patch systems, respond to incidents, and more," he said.

articles.title_orig: Tougher discipline, and Xi's authority, key at China's Communist Party's fifth plenum
articles.title_zh: Tougher discipline, and Xi's authority, key at China's Communist Party's fifth plenum
articles.content_orig:
Oct 23 (Reuters) - The elite Central Committee of China's ruling Communist Party holds a closed-door meeting in Beijing from Monday to ‌Thursday that will set the political tone ahead of late 2027's ‌once-every-five years party congress, and potentially discuss key personnel moves.
Here are some key facts about ​the plenum and how it works.
• The meeting is the fifth time the roughly 300 full and alternate members of China's Central Committee — the largest of the party's top decision-making bodies — have gathered since 2022's congress confirmed top ‌leader Xi Jinping's norm-breaking third ⁠term in office
• While the official theme is tightening discipline in the party's ranks, key personnel deliberations and what ⁠to do about disgraced former officials are also likely to feature prominently
• To prevent leaks, plenum attendees are traditionally confined to the venue for the duration of ​the ​meeting
• Little, if any, news of the ​proceedings is made public until ‌it closes. Foreign media and most Chinese reporters are given no access
• On the day the plenum closes, the official Xinhua news agency is expected to issue a dispatch, giving details of what was agreed, albeit typically full of opaque party terminology
• To portray party unity, there will almost ‌certainly be no mention of any disagreements ​within the senior leadership
• A more detailed document ​will usually follow several ​days later
• Past plenums have been held under tight security ‌at the Soviet-era Jingxi Hotel in ​western Beijing. The ​location of this year's meeting has not been announced
• The mood at plenums can vary greatly, depending on the agenda. A watershed conclave in ​1978 overseen by Deng ‌Xiaoping kick-started China's economic reforms, beginning the transformation of the ​country from a centrally planned backwater to an economic powerhouse
(Reporting by ​Beijing newsroom; Editing by Kate Mayberry)

articles.title_orig: Why Serbian elections are so important - as students challenge 12 years of Vučić rule
articles.title_zh: Why Serbian elections are so important - as students challenge 12 years of Vučić rule
articles.content_orig:
Final campaign rallies have taken place across Serbia, ahead of a snap election billed as a referendum on the country's future.
After two years of student protests, Serbians vote for a new parliament on Sunday in elections that threaten populist leader Aleksandar Vučić's 12 years in power.
The main threat to Vučić's dominance in Serbian politics comes from a two-year-old student movement, but there are concerns surrounding the fairness of the vote.
They have no obvious leaders and are not used to politics, but the "Student List-Students Win" movement has attracted anti-government voters across Serbia.
The Student List is fielding candidates from across Serbian society - and as he joined students marching towards Belgrade, lead candidate and cardiologist Ilija Srdanović said history was being rewritten: "The energy is unstoppable."
It all began on 1 November 2024, when the concrete canopy collapsed outside Novi Sad train station, in Serbia's second biggest city, killing 16 people.
The tragedy was seen as emblematic of corruption and negligence in Serbia. Critics linked the station's fatally flawed renovation to a president who had closely associated himself with the project.
What started as weekly student protests demanding justice on university campuses and city streets soon became a national movement, often at a local level, that encompassed far more sections of Serbian society, including farmers, actors and judges.
The Serbian Progressive party (SNS), founded by Vučić, was shaken and within weeks the prime minister resigned. Belgrade saw one of its biggest ever protests in March 2025, and while the leaderless student movement increased in strength, they organised themselves through student assemblies or plenums.
At the last election in 2023, Vučić's SNS was challenged by a loose coalition of pro-EU parties, that later fell apart. This time he faces a far clearer threat from a student movement that has shunned the mainstream opposition parties.
Vučić has spent two terms as president and cannot seek a third term, so he is now leading his party with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017 .
The right-wing populist leader has doubled down on unfounded allegations that his opponents are not so much students and professors, but "mighty great powers" seeking to overthrow Serbia. And he has vowed an end to what he sees as the politicisation of schools and universities.
Vučić has steered a careful path with the West, continuing to back Serbia's candidacy for the European Union, while refusing to impose sanctions on Russia for its full-scale war in Ukraine. Several government ministers attended the Belgrade funeral of war criminal Ratko Mladić, prompting EU anger at his "glorification".
Helena Ivanov of the Henry Jackson Society, a foreign policy think tank, says the students have been able to mobilise the masses in a way traditional opposition parties have not been able to - and this is Vučić's biggest challenge since he came to power.
"He's been running in all elections Serbia has had since the introduction of multi-party election system - so obviously defeating him isn't going to be easy, but this time around President Vučić isn't going to have an easy time either," she told the BBC from Belgrade.
Serbia has a parliament with 250 seats and there is just one national constituency under proportional representation.
Voting runs from 07:00 (06:00 GMT) and ends at 20:00 on Sunday.
There are 6.45 million registered voters and anyone over the age of 18 gets the right to choose which party's list of candidates to vote for.
Sunday's vote involves 18 lists but only seven of them are fielding the full 250 candidates. MPs are elected according to how much support the list receives if it wins more than 3% of the vote.
Several opposition parties have pulled out in favour of the Student List.
Far from being students themselves, the candidates are made up of teachers and university professors, actors and doctors, farmers and scientists.
They still have no leaders, but top candidate Ilija Srdanović is a cardiology professor in Novi Sad, while others include ex-basketball star Dejan Bodiroga, renowned actor Tihomir Stanić and former National Bank of Serbia governor Dejan Šoškić.

Vučić and the SNS party deny corruption and seeking to influence the media.
European observers are monitoring Sunday's vote, but even beforehand the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) has spoken of a "tense and divisive electoral climate" and a "referendum-like atmosphere".
Serbia's election commission says elections are free and the ballot is secret. However, independent watchdog CRTA has warned of a campaign that has seen threats and physical violence , and opposition activists subjected to surveillance.
In a report ahead of the vote, it said instead of ensuring equal conditions for candidates, "a range of institutions, from ministries to local governments, became involved in electoral engineering".
Serbian media has seen almost three-quarters of TV coverage devoted to government representatives, the watchdog complained, and alleged that ministries and local governments had become caught up in "electoral engineering".
Some 160 attacks have been recorded on media and journalists in Serbia this year, says the European Centre for Press and Media Freedom.

articles.title_orig: Uzbekistan strengthens its relations with China and US
articles.title_zh: Uzbekistan strengthens its relations with China and US
articles.content_orig:
In recent days, Uzbekistan welcomed the Chinese and American governments in quick succession.
During Chinese Premier Li Qiang’s visit on 17-18 October, the Uzbek presidential administration said that joint projects backed by firm agreements had reached nearly $60 billion.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio then arrived in Samarkand for C5+1 talks, accompanied at the time by American business leaders seeking contracts, particularly in critical minerals. During the visit, Uzbekistan announced 54 agreements covering trade, investment, and technology. The agreements are said to be worth a total of $12 billion, according to Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade. However, China still accounts for 23% of Uzbekistan’s foreign trade in January-August 2026, while US goods trade with Uzbekistan totalled at $1.05 billion in 2025, which is less than a fifteenth of the value of its trade with China. Rubio said Washington was not asking Central Asian countries to stop cooperating with other partners, but would instead compete for investment.
Tashkent is likely to welcome investment from both sides, but the trade gap shows how challenging it will be if it were to decrease its dependence on Beijing.
“Chinese Premier Li Qiang visited Uzbekistan on October 17–18, just ahead of United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who arrived in Samarkand on October 18 with a delegation of American business leaders seeking new contracts.
While China already has a substantial presence in Uzbek manufacturing and energy, Washington is seeking to expand American involvement in critical minerals and technology. The visits highlight the growing competition between the world’s two largest economies for influence in Central Asia.
On October 17, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev received Li Qiang. According to the Uzbek presidential administration, the portfolio of joint projects backed by firm agreements has reached nearly $60 billion. More than 6,000 joint ventures with Chinese participation have been established in Uzbekistan. (...) Construction of the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway was another topic of discussion. Work officially began in December 2024. The route will cross mountainous areas of Kyrgyzstan and connect the railway networks of China and Uzbekistan. The 304-kilometer section through Kyrgyzstan alone is estimated to cost $4.7 billion and will require 50 bridges and 29 tunnels. (...)
On October 19, Rubio attended talks in Samarkand under the C5+1 format, bringing together the U.S. and Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan. Rubio said nearly 300 American businesses were represented in Samarkand. Companies were discussing agreements potentially worth billions of dollars, with concrete announcements expected following the meetings. Among Washington’s priorities are critical minerals used in advanced technologies, including electronics and batteries.”
source: Caucasus and Central Asia Concise Vol 1 No 6 with Times of Central Asia

articles.content_orig:

(Bloomberg) -- US Treasuries are showing tentative signs of reclaiming their traditional role as a haven — threatening to wrong-foot investors who are heavily positioned for this year's bond slump to deepen.
